issues.title: Cost-aware initial scan filter order: run Bloom/dynamic join filters after cheap constant predicates
issues.hypothesis: Most of q19's time is the lineitem TABLE_SCAN (4.05-6.18s cumulative, ~85%). Standalone A/Bs in one dbe-tool session show the Bloom-filter join filter on l_partkey is the most expensive filter per row: BF-only scan 2.44s cum (349ms wall), shipinstruct-eq + quantity-OR without BF 1.57s (204ms), all three together 2.09s (286ms). Adding cheap selective predicates made the scan cheaper because less hashing was done. ExpressionHeuristics::Cost(const TableFilter&) (src/optimizer/expression_heuristics.cpp:225) gives OPTIONAL_FILTER/DYNAMIC_FILTER a cost of 0, so the l_partkey filter AND(opt>=, opt<=, opt BF) costs 5. That ties with the VARCHAR equality (ExpressionCost(VARCHAR,1)=5). EXPRESSION_FILTER falls to default 1000. The TableFilterSet map is keyed by scan column index, and the l_partkey column comes before l_shipinstruct. GetInitialOrder's sort on 4 elements is an insertion sort and keeps that order, so the initial permutation is [shipmode(always-true), partkey-BF, shipinstruct, quantity]. That means the BF hashes and probes all ~60M rows instead of the ~25% that pass shipinstruct. AdaptiveFilter (src/execution/adaptive_filter.cpp) can only fix this with random swaps judged on noisy 10-vector wall timings. One of the 3 swap slots involves the always-true shipmode filter, so those swaps are no-ops. Giving the BF a realistic, higher cost, and giving SelectivityOptionalFilter its child's cost, puts the BF after cheap comparisons from the first vector.
issues.plan:
In src/optimizer/expression_heuristics.cpp, ExpressionHeuristics::Cost(const TableFilter &filter):
(1) case BLOOM_FILTER: return a hash-plus-probe cost, e.g. 50. That is above simple constant comparisons (1-5) and below generic expressions.
(2) case OPTIONAL_FILTER: if dynamic_cast<const SelectivityOptionalFilter *>(&filter) succeeds (include duckdb/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.hpp), return Cost(*child_filter), because it really filters. A plain OptionalFilter stays 0, since it is skipped anyway.
(3) Optional, only if (1)+(2) alone do not reorder q19: EXPRESSION_FILTER returns Cost(*expr_filter.expr) via the existing Expression cost instead of 1000. Then a numeric OR-of-ranges (~104) is no longer treated as maximally expensive.
Keep DYNAMIC_FILTER at 0. Change nothing in AdaptiveFilter.
Verify with an A/B on the same build (temporarily switch the new branch on and off, or compare against the current best with bench run twice): the q19 lineitem scan cumulative time in `dbe-tool profile q19.m0`, then bench q19. Also sanity-check `SELECT sum(l_extendedprice) FROM lineitem WHERE l_partkey IN (SELECT p_partkey FROM part WHERE p_size<=5 AND p_brand='Brand#45')` (BF-only), so a scan where the BF is the only filter is unaffected.
issues.expected_gain: q19: if the BF currently runs first on all rows, moving it after the 25%-selective string equality should cut BF hash/probe work ~4x. Estimate -10..-25% q19. It is 0% if AdaptiveFilter had already converged to that order (then retire, and note that ordering is not the bottleneck).
issues.generality: Any scan probing a hash-join build where the scan also has cheap local constant predicates: star joins, TPC-H Q3/Q5/Q9/Q10/Q12/Q19-like shapes. This affects only the initial filter permutation, and AdaptiveFilter can still swap at runtime. It could get slightly slower when local predicates are unselective and the BF is very selective, but SelectivityOptionalFilter and adaptive swaps limit that. Results cannot change, because filter order does not affect correctness.
issues.risk: Low. It only reorders conjunctive table filters, and all of them are evaluated anyway. dynamic_cast on TableFilter is polymorphic and safe. The main risk is no measurable gain within bench noise (~5-10%).
